title: Evaluating Controls for Trading Compliance: An Offline Study of Order Splitting and Cancellation Timing
abstract: An order-by-order size limit can admit a large display assembled from smaller orders. We built ConductLab, a custom limit-order-book simulator and replay workflow, to examine this gap while separating alerts, gains from the simulated price response, and costs to legitimate execution. Six 10-lot orders pass the original gate without a conduct alert in all 40 tested seeds. An aggregate cap removes the gain at the original settings, but its effect depends on the assumed response. With throttling disabled, the same 20-lot cap gives a mean responsive-minus-unresponsive wealth difference of 0.00 tick-lots at threshold 0.4 and 48.00 at 0.2. Checks on either side of the response boundary preserve this contrast. The full policy reduces volume by 14.1% for a large maker and 28.2% for a patient maker; a separate ablation attributes most of the large maker's loss to throttling. In a one-hour test, submissions resume after lockout but volume remains 75.2% below the ungated baseline. A legitimate maker triggers alerts in 39/40 episodes at a 170-second quoting interval and 0/40 at 190 seconds, with a 180-second detector window. These scripted cases expose control interactions that can be obscured by reporting alerts alone. The prices are synthetic; the results describe the implemented rules and their consequences, not real-market detection accuracy.
comments: 13 pages, 3 figures; exploratory scripted simulation study
assessment: Suitable for release only as a bounded exploratory methods report; independent strategy validation, market calibration, and LLM evidence remain absent.
